facts: The current red sandstone castle dates from the 1830s, built on the site of earlier fortifications.
Inverness is often called the capital of the Highlands.
The castle overlooks the River Ness as it flows towards the Moray Firth.
Culloden was the site of the final Jacobite defeat in 1746, ending Bonnie Prince Charlie's rising.
The battle lasted less than an hour but caused around 1,500 Jacobite casualties.
Inverness is the nearest railhead, with the battlefield reached by bus or car.
Loch Ness holds more freshwater than every lake in England and Wales combined.
Urquhart Castle's ruins sit on the loch's shore and were once one of the largest castles in Scotland.
Inverness, at the northern end of the loch, is the main gateway for visitors.
Dunrobin Castle has its own private railway station, opened for the Duke of Sutherland in 1870.
With over 100 rooms, it is one of the largest houses in Scotland, resembling a French chateau.
The castle has been the seat of the Earls and Dukes of Sutherland for centuries.
The Cairngorms is the largest national park in the UK, covering over 4,500 square kilometres.
Aviemore is the main gateway town, with a funicular railway climbing part of Cairn Gorm mountain.
The Strathspey Railway, a heritage steam line, also runs from Aviemore.
Blair Castle is the seat of the Duke of Atholl, whose private army is the only legal one in Britain.
The white harled castle has been added to and altered since the 13th century.
Blair Atholl station sits on the Highland Main Line between Perth and Inverness.
Scone Palace was the crowning place of Scottish kings, including Robert the Bruce and Macbeth.
The Stone of Scone, used in coronations, was kept here before being moved to Westminster and later Edinburgh.
Perth was historically known as 'the Fair City' and served as an early capital of Scotland.
The dam's fish ladder allows migrating salmon to bypass the hydroelectric dam via an observation chamber.
Pitlochry Festival Theatre stages a full repertoire of productions each summer season.
The town sits in the scenic Pass of Killiecrankie, site of a 1689 Jacobite battle.
Discovery Point displays the RRS Discovery, the ship that carried Captain Scott's 1901 Antarctic expedition.
Dundee was once the world's leading producer of jute textiles, alongside jam and journalism.
The city's V&A Dundee, opened in 2018, was Scotland's first design museum.
The Declaration of Arbroath, a key document asserting Scottish independence, was sealed at the abbey in 1320.
Arbroath is also famous for the Arbroath Smokie, a traditionally smoked haddock with protected status.
The abbey ruins stand near the town's harbour.
Dunnottar Castle sits dramatically on a rocky headland above the North Sea.
The Scottish Crown Jewels were hidden here to protect them from Cromwell's forces in the 1650s.
Stonehaven is the nearest station, with the castle reached along the coast path.
Montrose Basin is a large tidal basin important for wintering geese and wading birds.
It is designated a Site of Special Scientific Interest and a Local Nature Reserve.
Montrose is one of the oldest royal burghs in Scotland.

landmark: Kyle of Lochalsh & the Skye Bridge
facts: The Skye Bridge, opened in 1995, replaced a centuries-old ferry crossing to the Isle of Skye.
Kyle of Lochalsh is the terminus of one of Britain's most scenic railway lines, from Inverness.
The line was famously featured in a BBC documentary as one of the great railway journeys of the world.
Eilean Donan is one of the most photographed castles in Scotland, sitting on its own tidal island.
The castle was destroyed in 1719 and not restored until the early 20th century.
Plockton, a picturesque fishing village, is the nearest station on the Kyle of Lochalsh line.
Elgin Cathedral, once known as 'the Lantern of the North', was one of the finest medieval cathedrals in Scotland.
It was burned in 1390 by Alexander Stewart, the notorious 'Wolf of Badenoch'.
Elgin sits at the heart of Speyside, Scotland's whisky-producing heartland.
Strathisla is the oldest continuously operating distillery in the Scottish Highlands, founded in 1786.
Keith sits at the heart of Speyside, home to more whisky distilleries than anywhere else in the world.
The town is linked to Dufftown by the heritage Keith and Dufftown Railway.
Fort George is one of the most outstanding artillery fortifications in Europe, built after Culloden.
It remains an active army barracks as well as a visitor attraction.
Nairn is a Victorian seaside resort, nicknamed 'the Brighton of the North'.
Cawdor Castle is associated with Shakespeare's Macbeth, though the current building postdates the historical king.
The castle has been the home of the Thanes of Cawdor since the 14th century.
Nairn is a genteel seaside town with two golf courses and long sandy beaches.
John o' Groats is popularly, though not technically accurately, considered the northernmost point of mainland Britain.
It marks one end of the famous Land's End to John o' Groats route, the longest distance between two inhabited points in the UK.
Wick is the terminus of the Far North Line, one of the longest and most remote rail journeys in Britain.
Old Pulteney is often nicknamed 'the Maritime Malt' for its coastal, salty character.
Wick was once the busiest herring fishing port in Europe during the 19th century.
The town's Pulteneytown district was purpose-built by Thomas Telford for fishing families.

landmark: Dunnet Head & Britain's most northerly point
facts: Dunnet Head is the actual most northerly point of the British mainland, further north than John o' Groats.
Thurso is the northernmost town on the British mainland and terminus of the Far North Line.
The Orkney ferry departs from nearby Scrabster, a short distance from Thurso.
Beauly Priory was founded in 1230 for the Valliscaulian order of monks.
The town's name is said to come from the French 'beau lieu', meaning beautiful place.
Beauly station reopened in 2002 after closure decades earlier, on the line towards Kyle of Lochalsh.
Glenmorangie's stills are among the tallest in Scotland, giving the whisky its light, delicate character.
Tain is one of Scotland's oldest royal burghs, with a charter dating to 1066.
The town sits on the Dornoch Firth in Easter Ross.
Invergordon's deep-water harbour on the Cromarty Firth has serviced North Sea oil rigs since the 1970s.
The town was a major Royal Navy base in both World Wars.
The Cromarty Firth is also a popular anchorage for cruise ships visiting the Highlands.
Huntly Castle was the seat of the powerful Gordon family, Marquesses of Huntly.
Its ruins feature elaborate heraldic carvings above the main entrance.
Huntly sits at the junction of the Rivers Deveron and Bogie.
Aberdeen's Maritime Museum tells the story of the city's fishing, shipbuilding and North Sea oil industries.
Aberdeen is nicknamed the 'Granite City' for the light grey stone used in much of its architecture.
The city has been a major hub for North Sea oil and gas since the 1970s.
Aberdeen Airport at Dyce is one of the world's busiest heliports, serving North Sea oil platforms.
Dyce was originally a separate village before being absorbed into the city of Aberdeen.
The station serves both the airport and Aberdeen's northern business district.
Inverurie sits at the confluence of the Rivers Don and Urie, in the heart of Aberdeenshire farmland.
The town's Bass, a prehistoric mound, may have been used as a medieval motte.
Inverurie is a key stop between Aberdeen and Inverness.
Insch sits beneath the Correen Hills in rural Aberdeenshire.
The area is dotted with prehistoric standing stones and stone circles.
Insch is a request stop on the line between Aberdeen and Inverness.
The nearby Highland Folk Museum recreates a working 1700s township and 1930s highland village.
Kingussie sits in Badenoch, within the Cairngorms National Park.
The town has one of Scotland's oldest shinty clubs, a traditional Highland sport.
Newtonmore's shinty club is one of the most successful in the sport's history.
The village sits at the meeting of the Rivers Spey and Calder.
Newtonmore is a gateway to walking routes into the Cairngorms.
Dalwhinnie is one of the highest distilleries in Scotland, at over 350 metres above sea level.
The village is often recorded as one of the coldest inhabited places in the UK.
Dalwhinnie sits at a historic crossroads of Highland drove roads.
The Old Bridge of Carr, built in 1717, is one of the oldest surviving bridges in the Highlands.
Carrbridge is also home to the Landmark Forest Adventure Park.
The village sits within the Cairngorms National Park, on the Highland Main Line.
Carbisdale Castle, overlooking Culrain, was built in the early 1900s for the Dowager Duchess of Sutherland.
It later served as a youth hostel, once the largest and grandest in Scotland.
Culrain sits on the Kyle of Sutherland, on the Far North Line.
Lairg sits at the southern end of Loch Shin, the largest freshwater loch in Sutherland.
The village hosts one of Europe's largest one-day livestock sales each August.
Lairg is a key junction point for roads across the Highlands.
The Sutherland Monument, above Golspie, honours the first Duke of Sutherland, a controversial figure linked to the Highland Clearances.
Golspie sits beside Dunrobin Castle, seat of the Sutherland family.
The village has a long sandy beach on the Moray Firth coast.
Helmsdale was the site of a brief Scottish gold rush in the 1860s, at nearby Kildonan.
The Timespan Museum in the village tells the story of Highland life and the Clearances.
Helmsdale sits at the mouth of the River Helmsdale on the North Sea coast.
Brora is home to one of Scotland's most northerly whisky distilleries still in regular production.
The village has a well-regarded links golf course along its sandy shoreline.
Brora was historically notable for its coal mining, unusual for such a northerly location.

landmark: Georgemas Junction, Britain's most northerly junction
facts: Georgemas Junction is the most northerly railway junction in Britain, splitting the line to Thurso and Wick.
The station has very few passengers of its own, mainly serving as an interchange point.
It sits in open Caithness farmland between Thurso and Wick.
Forsinard Flows protects the Flow Country, the largest expanse of blanket bog in Europe.
The peatlands here store more carbon than all the UK's forests combined.
Forsinard station sits in one of the most remote parts of mainland Britain.
Achnasheen is a remote junction settlement providing road access towards Torridon and the northwest Highlands.
The station sits on the scenic Kyle of Lochalsh line from Inverness.
The surrounding glen is renowned for dramatic mountain scenery.
Strathcarron provides road access to the remote Applecross peninsula via the Bealach na Ba pass.
The Bealach na Ba is one of the highest and steepest road climbs in Britain.
Strathcarron station sits on the Kyle of Lochalsh line.
Achnashellach Forest is a remnant of ancient Caledonian pine woodland.
The station is a request stop deep within Wester Ross.
It sits close to the Torridon mountain range, among the oldest rock formations in Europe.
Dundee Law is the plug of an extinct volcano rising above the city, offering panoramic views.
A war memorial stands at its summit, commemorating Dundee's fallen from both World Wars.
Dundee sits on the north bank of the Firth of Tay.
Broughty Castle, a 15th-century tower house, guards the mouth of the Firth of Tay.
Broughty Ferry was historically a fishing village before becoming a fashionable Dundee suburb.
The area is nicknamed 'the Beverly Hills of Dundee' for its Victorian villas.
Carnoustie has hosted The Open Championship multiple times and is considered one of golf's toughest tests.
The course's final hole, 'Home', is notorious among professional golfers for its difficulty.
Carnoustie sits on the Angus coast between Dundee and Arbroath.
St Andrews is home to the Old Course, widely regarded as the home of golf, dating back over 600 years.
The University of St Andrews, founded in 1413, is the oldest in Scotland.
Leuchars is the nearest railway station, with St Andrews reached by bus.
Laurencekirk was once known for a distinctive style of folding wooden ruler invented locally.
The town sits in the fertile agricultural region known as the Howe of the Mearns.
Laurencekirk station reopened in 2009 after closure decades earlier.
Cupar was historically the county town of Fife.
The nearby Hill of Tarvit mansion and gardens are cared for by the National Trust for Scotland.
Cupar sits between St Andrews and the Fife coastal fishing villages of the East Neuk.
The Dalmore distillery sits on the shore of the Cromarty Firth, near Alness.
Its distinctive stag-head still motif references a royal hunting story from the 1263 Battle of Largs.
Alness is a small town on the line between Inverness and the far north.
